races.note: The top two finishers from the Nov 3, 2026 count. Everyone else in this race is coming.

cands.name: Paul Barringer

money.note: Individuals gave $727,723; PAC money $10,000; candidate's own money $470,865. Percentages describe itemized individual gifts, which the FEC has processed through about July 2026.

cands.bio: Attorney and health care consultant with 20+ years working with state governments on Medicaid and public programs. Manages his family's tree farm in Lee County, provides pro bono Social Security disability legal help, and founded the Mill & Mountain clothing brand. Has not held elective office.
cands.gaps: We found no record of Barringer holding elected or appointed office, so there are no legislative actions to report. His birthplace and the year he may have moved to North Carolina were not found. We found no stated position from him on data centers, homestead property taxes, limits on institutional or foreign land buyers, or school vouchers and charters, and no direct statement on H-1B visas. We found no documented controversies, foreign ties or notable endorsements. The only endorsements listed were informal social-media voting groups.

qual.background: Attorney and healthcare consultant who has worked with state governments on Medicaid and public programs, also an entrepreneur and executive in the healthcare industry, family tree-farm manager, and pro bono Social Security disability lawyer; no prior elected office.
qual.why: He has law and state health-program policy experience and business management experience, but has held no legislative or executive office, so the score sits in the middle range.
qual.label: He has law and state health-program policy experience and business management experience, but has held no legislative or executive office, so the score sits in the middle range.

back-police-order.evidence: Said on his campaign website that he strongly supports law enforcement and wants officers to have the resources and respect they need, while also backing rehabilitation and re-entry programs.

workers-first.evidence: Said on his campaign website that he supports a secure border and smart, effective enforcement against illegal crossings. He also said the legal immigration system should be modernized to meet workforce needs, especially in agriculture, health care and tech. He did not mention H-1B specifically.

second-amendment.evidence: Said he is a gun owner who supports the Second Amendment, wants existing laws enforced, and is open to bipartisan 'common-sense solutions' to keep guns from dangerous individuals. He named no specific measure, and nothing on red-flag laws, suppressors or purchase ages.

pro-life.evidence: Said he wants to expand family planning and contraception access and support adoption and foster care, and that 'the law should not be an impediment to a woman making the health care choices she needs to make with her doctor.'

slow-growth-protect-land.evidence: Said he supports full funding for the Land and Water Conservation Fund, voluntary conservation easements on private land, preserving farmland, and protecting clean water and public lands.

clean-money.evidence: Said in his Ballotpedia survey that he is running to represent the district, 'not Donald Trump, party leadership, or billionaire donors,' and that he wants to reduce the influence of money in politics. He did not name a specific donation-refusal pledge.

prio.label: Matches 4 of 6 priorities; 0 backed by their record, 4 only promised

roots.summary: His campaign site says he grew up on a farm in Lee County and attended Lee County public schools, and he still lives on a farm there; his birthplace is not stated.

money.note: Individuals gave $573,207; PAC money $866,669; candidate's own money $0. Percentages describe itemized individual gifts, which the FEC has processed through about July 2026.

cands.bio: Republican attorney and U.S. Representative for North Carolina's 13th District since January 2025. A Raleigh native, he was a federal prosecutor in the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Eastern District of North Carolina from 2016 to November 2023. He first ran for office in 2024.

controversies.text: Federal records show $20,000 from AIPAC's PAC since 2021; $17,050 from individuals passed through that PAC in 2025-26; 1 staff trip paid for by that foundation.
Missed 11 of 676 U.S. House votes this Congress (1.6%), counted from the roll calls through 2026-09-16. Longest run of misses: 2, 2026-07-20 to 2026-07-20.

WRAL reported in February 2024 that Knott was registered to vote at his parents' Raleigh address from 2010 to 2023. He voted in five general elections from that address after buying his own home in 2014. Knott said it "slipped my mind" and called it a paperwork issue. WRAL said no one had challenged his ballots.

endorsements.text: Donald Trump endorsed him in 2024 and 2026.
U.S. Sen. Ted Budd endorsed him in 2024.
Americans for Prosperity endorsed him in the 2024 Republican runoff.

cands.gaps: We found no documented positions or actions from Knott on data centers, development or growth, homestead property taxes, limits on foreign or investor land buying, H-1B visas, or teacher pay. We found no pledge on refusing particular kinds of donations. He did not complete Ballotpedia's candidate survey in 2024 or 2026. We could not read the news reporting behind the voter-registration criticism, so only the brief account on Wikipedia is included.

votes.what: Final FY2026 spending package funding most remaining federal agencies through September 30, 2026.

votes.bill: S. 1071 / FY2026 National Defense Authorization Act (final)
votes.what: Final FY2026 defense policy and funding-authorization bill (about $900 billion), carried in the House on the vehicle S. 1071.

votes.bill: H.R. 5371 (2025) Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2026 (Nov. 12 final, ended the shutdown)
votes.what: Ended the 43-day federal shutdown: funds government through Jan. 30, 2026 and three full-year spending bills.

votes.bill: H.R. 5371 (2025) Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2026 (Sept. 19 House passage)
votes.what: House-passed stopgap funding bill to keep government open through Nov. 21, 2025; stalled in the Senate and a shutdown began Oct. 1.

votes.bill: H.R. 1 (2025) One Big Beautiful Bill Act (final passage)
votes.what: The 2025 reconciliation law: extends the 2017 tax cuts, adds new tax breaks, cuts Medicaid and food-assistance spending, and raises defense and border spending and the debt limit.

votes.bill: H.R. 881 (2025) DHS Restrictions on Confucius Institutes and Chinese Entities of Concern Act
votes.what: Bars Homeland Security funds going to Confucius Institutes and entities tied to the Chinese government.
Requires documentary proof of U.S. citizenship to register to vote in federal elections.

votes.bill: H.R. 1968 (2025) Full-Year Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2025
votes.what: Funds the federal government through September 30, 2025 at roughly prior-year levels (March 2025 stopgap).

votes.bill: H.R. 152 (2025) Federal Disaster Assistance Coordination Act
votes.what: Streamlines coordination among federal agencies delivering disaster aid (hurricane/flood recovery).
Requires federal detention of undocumented immigrants charged with theft, burglary or assault of a police officer, and lets states sue over immigration enforcement.

qual.background: Federal prosecutor in the U.S. Attorney's Office for Eastern North Carolina from 2016 to November 2023, after clerking for NC Supreme Court Justice Paul Newby during law school. He has served in the U.S. House since January 2025, with seats on the Homeland Security, Judiciary and Transportation and Infrastructure committees.
qual.why: Seven and a half years as a federal prosecutor plus a current term in the U.S. House put him in the high range for a lawmaking and oversight job. The committee seats themselves were not counted.
qual.label: Seven and a half years as a federal prosecutor plus a current term in the U.S. House put him in the high range for a lawmaking and oversight job. The committee seats themselves were not counted.

workers-first.evidence: Voted Yea on the Laken Riley Act, which requires DHS to detain certain people in the U.S. without legal permission who are arrested for burglary, theft, larceny or shoplifting; it became law on 1/29/2025.

pro-life.evidence: Says he is pro-life, supports state laws protecting the unborn, and will fight to protect faith-based crisis pregnancy centers. He says Dobbs properly returned abortion authority to the states.

school-choice-teachers.evidence: Says he supports school choice so parents can move children out of failing schools. His site does not mention teacher pay.

second-amendment.evidence: Says he will protect the right to keep and bear arms and that existing gun laws should be enforced rather than new ones passed that target law-abiding citizens.

back-police-order.evidence: Says he backs the blue '100%' and supports tough-on-crime policies, citing his work with sheriffs and police as a prosecutor.
